title: Olivia Wilde Brings a Dinner Party From Hell to Indian Screens. Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton Are Already RSVP'd.
excerpt: A24's slinky, 91%-fresh Sundance hit The Invite lands in Indian theatres this summer — four magnetic stars, one apartment, and a proposition that could reignite a marriage or torch it.
body:
The trailer opens with a doorbell and a bottle of wine, and by the time it ends you're not sure which of these four beautiful, dangerous people you should be more afraid of. That's the trick of The Invite, Olivia Wilde's third film as a director, and it's coming to Indian theatres this summer courtesy of PVRINOX Pictures.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=OJ19I9q_hOQ

Here's the setup, and it's deliciously simple. Joe (Seth Rogen) and Angela (Wilde herself) are a married couple on thin ice — the kind of quiet, polite ice where nobody's slammed a door yet but everybody's thinking about it. To shake things loose, they invite the upstairs neighbours down for dinner. Enter Hawk (Edward Norton) and Pína (Penélope Cruz) — older, glossier, unnervingly comfortable in their own skin, and carrying an invitation of their own. "Have they reignited the spark," the official logline teases, "or lit the match that burns it all down?"

https://x.com/NewYorker/status/2068438966794432780
"Cruz at 51 is in the prime-vixen phase of a career that has never once looked ordinary, and the trailer lets her smoulder."
"I found myself wrestling with the themes of the original as though I were in a relationship with it. It became this intense obsession." — Olivia Wilde

!Olivia Wilde — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

This is A24 doing what A24 does best: take a single apartment, four of the most watchable actors alive, and let the tension marinate. Cruz at 51 is in the prime-vixen phase of a career that has never once looked ordinary, and the trailer lets her smoulder. Norton brings that coiled, too-charming menace he's perfected. Rogen plays against type as the anxious husband watching his marriage get appraised at his own dinner table. And Wilde, behind and in front of the camera, frames the whole thing like a chamber thriller dressed up as a comedy — scored, in the trailer at least, to a knowing rendition of Anita Ward's "Ring My Bell."

It is, in the most flattering sense, a film about adults behaving badly. And it earned its stripes the hard way. The Invite premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival in January, drew a standing ovation, left Wilde wiping away tears during the post-screening Q&A, and walked away with a 91% Rotten Tomatoes score and a 77 on Metacritic. After the divided reception to her 2022 thriller Don't Worry Darling, this is the comeback Wilde needed — and critics handed it to her.

The film is an English-language remake of Cesc Gay's sharp 2020 Spanish comedy The People Upstairs (Sentimental), reworked by the Celeste and Freaks and Geeks-adjacent writing duo Rashida Jones and Will McCormack. Wilde shot the whole thing in a brisk 23 days in May 2025 with, in her words, "some of the greatest humans ever made." The economy shows in the best way — this is lean, talky, claustrophobic filmmaking where every glance does work.

Where the diaspora comes in. For NRI audiences who've been starved of grown-up Hollywood comedy on the big screen, this is the rare imported title getting a proper theatrical push in India. PVRINOX is releasing it across Indian multiplexes, with the date settling around the film's wider expansion window — A24 opens it limited in the US on June 26 before going broad in July, and the India theatrical run is slated for early-to-mid July. For viewers in the US, UK and Canada, A24 titles typically reach premium VOD within weeks of the theatrical run, with a streaming home (often Max or the studio's distribution partners) following later in the year — so if the multiplex isn't an option, patience pays.

The smart money says this plays beautifully to the urban Indian and diaspora crowd that made Marriage Story and The Worst Person in the World dinner-table conversation. It's verbal, it's flirtatious, it's about the precise anxieties of modern coupledom — situationships, boredom, the terror of being truly seen by the person across the table. Sound familiar? It should. It's the same emotional terrain Bollywood's been mining all summer, just with a colder cocktail and a darker punchline.

Four stars. One apartment. One night that goes somewhere nobody planned. Pour the wine, lock the door, and watch four magnetic people decide whether to save their marriages or set them on fire. The Invite is one dinner party worth crashing.
